blocks.explanation:
Same idea as Question 6: a root is a fractional power, \(\sqrt[k]{x} = x^{1/k}\).
Writing 16, 64, 256 as powers of 4 turns the product into \(4^S\), with the same infinite A.G.P. \(S\).
Plan: roots to powers, everything as a power of 4, find \(S\), work out \(4^S\).
steps:
Given: \(\sqrt{4} \cdot \sqrt[4]{16} \cdot \sqrt[8]{64} \cdot \sqrt[16]{256} \cdots\)
To find: show that the product equals 16.
Method: \(\sqrt[k]{x} = x^{\frac1k}\), laws of indices, and the A.G.P. method for the sum of the powers.

Change roots into powers
\[\text{L.H.S.} = 4^{\frac12} \cdot 16^{\frac14} \cdot 64^{\frac18} \cdot 256^{\frac{1}{16}} \cdots\]
Why: The \(k\)th root is the power \(\frac1k\).

Write every base as a power of 4
\[16 = 4^{2},\ 64 = 4^{3},\ 256 = 4^{4}\]
\[= 4^{\frac12} (4^{2})^{\frac14}\]
\[\quad \times (4^{3})^{\frac18} (4^{4})^{\frac{1}{16}} \cdots\]
\[= 4^{\frac12 + \frac24 + \frac38 + \frac{4}{16} + \cdots}\]
\[= 4^{S}\]
Why: Power of a power multiplies; same base: add the powers.

Sum the powers (an infinite A.G.P.)
\[S = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{2}{4} + \dfrac{3}{8} + \dfrac{4}{16} + \cdots\]
\[\tfrac{1}{2}S = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{2}{8} + \dfrac{3}{16} + \cdots\]
\[\tfrac{1}{2}S = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \cdots\]
\[= \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} = 1\]
\[S = 2\]
Why: The powers \(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{2}{4}, \frac{3}{8}, \ldots\) have tops \(1, 2, 3, \ldots\) (A.P.) and bottoms \(2, 4, 8, \ldots\) (G.P., \(r = \frac12\)). Multiply by \(\frac12\), shift and subtract; each pair leaves 1 on top. The result is an infinite G.P. with first term \(\frac12\), ratio \(\frac12\), sum 1; so \(S = 2\).

Work out the product
\[\text{L.H.S.} = 4^{S} = 4^{2} = 16 = \text{R.H.S.}\]
Why: Put \(S = 2\).
